newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Enel, Enron plan electricity link-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Enel, Enron plan electricity link-up.

text.p: Italian utility firm Enel plans to join forces with U.S. giant Enron Corp to create a major independent electricity generator ahead of the liberalisation of the domestic market, industrial sources said on Tuesday.

The sources said the two companies would sign a letter of intent later on Tuesday to prepare the way for a 50-50 joint venture with generating assets of a maximum 5,000 megawatts, worth around $3.0 billion.

It will be the second time in a month that Ente Nazionale per l'Energia Elettrica (Enel) has decided to hive off a chunk its existing 55,000 megawatt capacity in preparation for the opening of the Italian electricity distribution market in 1999.
Sources said that state-owned Enel would provide all the generating power for the Enron venture and would place around $2.4 billion of its debt in the company.
The European unit of Houston-based Enron, one of the world's largest natural gas and electricity groups, will inject cash into the project, the sources said.

Full financial plans have not been worked out and no details are expected in the letter of intent. However the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Enron and Enel would each contribute $300 million of equity in the venture.
Last month, Enel announced it was linking up with Italian energy group Eni to create an electricity production company with a similar capacity to the Enron initiative.

The firm will eventually be floated on international stock exchanges and Enel chairman Chicco Testa said last week that General Electric Co of the U.S. had expressed an interest in buying a stake in the group.
It was not clear if the Enron/Enel operation would also be floated or open to third parties.

The Eni/Enel deal infuriated Italy's small independent electricity production sector, with private companies complaining that the two state controlled groups were looking to take a stranglehold on the liberalised market.

Enel currently enjoys a monopoly over domestic distribution, but around 30 percent of the market will opened to independent companies following European Union demands that the Italian electricity sector be freed up.
"The philosophy behind the ventures is for Enel to be able to compete in the liberalised market," an industry source said.

Enel, which recently announced record profits of 1.27 trillion lire ($747 million) for 1996, was due to be privatised by the end of the year, but the flotation has been postponed and no new timetable set with the government undecided how to sell the company.
Some sector specialists have argued that it should be split into its various production, distribution and transmission activities, but unions are fighting to keep it in one piece.
